segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: My wife told me about this thing that-- honestly, this is news to me. You know when it's like the height of summer and you go out, and a feeling when the sun is just like really hot and hitting your skin and making you all warm? She likes that feeling. She likes the way that feels.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I don't know what this says about me, but the notion that anybody would like that had never occurred to me. Totally eye opening because I have never been into that feeling at all. To me, the heat of summer is just something you had to get through. It was like rain, but less wet.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And since she said this, this summer I've been trying to practice it. I've been trying to reprogram my own experience of the summer. And so when I'm outside, I consciously tell myself, the sun's hitting me. I'm going to enjoy this, get into it. And I can kind of get myself there for a little while. And then I lose it. I can't hold onto it. I just think that some of us really love the summer. And it is not something that you can force.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A couple weeks ago here on our radio show, we all saw this article about somebody like that. He's a 66-year-old lifeguard who's suing New York State for age discrimination. And I just want to pause on that for a second, a 66-year-old lifeguard.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: All of us here on our staff, we had no idea that could even exist. We all thought lifeguarding is something that you do when you're in high school, maybe a couple years after, into your 20s. Who is still lifeguarding at 66?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then it was even more of a question when we realized the lifeguard in the story, he has another job. He's a lawyer. He's a working lawyer.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: His name is Roy Lester. He's a bankruptcy attorney. He's got his own firm in Long Island. And then he lifeguards every weekend in the summer.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And today on our program, we have stories of people like him, people who love the summer, not people like me. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. We prepared today a program to listen to with the sun beating down on you, the humidity through the roof, a show of people embracing summer and everything about summer. And let's just get right to it with Act One.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, The Grapes of Wrath. So one of our producers, Dana Chivvis, she went out to Long Island and met that guy, Roy Lester, the 66-year-old attorney lifeguard who was suing New York State. Basically the deal is that they tried to make him wear a Speedo. He refused. He lost his job. Here's Dana.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: If you ask Roy, why are you still lifeguarding at 66, he barely understands the question. It's so self-evident to him. It's been his life since he was 16. He and his buddies were kings of the beach. He lived with other lifeguards. His best man at his wedding was a lifeguard. Their kids grew up playing together on the beach while they were on duty. He never wanted to leave this job. Even when he went to law school in California, he came back to lifeguard every summer.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: In law school, aren't you supposed to have an internship in a law firm or something like that?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: You're supposed to.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Did you not do that?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: No, I did not do that. I never took it quite that seriously. The idea of giving up the summer was something I just couldn't do.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: He's not alone. At Jones Beach, where he worked for 40 years, there are dozens of guys-- teachers, firemen, police-- who stayed with it into their 60s. Lifeguarding at Jones Beach is such a thing that a former lifeguard made a film about it. It's called Jones Beach Boys .

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Roy insisted I watch it. I did. It was awesome. Here's my favorite song from it.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: [MUSIC PLAYING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: "We're going for the rescue and getting to the victim." I never really appreciated how thrilling lifeguarding is until Roy talked about rescues. We were sitting in his law office.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: The exhilaration of a good rescue is unlike anything you've ever had. And you don't get that. I sit here, and I shuffle papers. I wouldn't call it exciting. I wouldn't call it rewarding.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: But this is-- you're actually accomplishing something. You're up there, and all of a sudden you're going out in the water, and the rest of the world is behind you. There's nothing else except between you getting from your stand to that victim. That's the only thing. And it's great. It's a great feeling.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: How many people do you think you've rescued in your career?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Over 1,000.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Yeah. You have to remember. There were times we would have 40 rescues in an hour.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: What? Why? What? Who? Why?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Because you have people that come down to Jones Beach who really don't know about swimming, especially when you have a current. And you can get a very strong current at Jones Beach.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: 1,000 rescues-- that's way more rescues than David Hasselhoff did on Baywatch . I figure two rescues per episode, 10 years on the air, Roy would still beat him by 560 rescues.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Which is to say Roy is one of the lifeguardiest lifeguards there is. He had two wins at the national lifeguard competition. He served as an expert lifeguard witness in court cases. And all was well in his happy lifeguarding world until the Speedo mishegoss began in 2007.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Here's what happened. If you're a lifeguard at Jones Beach, you have to take a physical fitness test every year to prove that you're still able to do the job. It includes a speed test in a pool. You have to swim 100 yards in 1:20, which is actually pretty fast. A lot of these guys train all year for it.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: For 15 years, Roy took the swim test in his preferred swimsuit, a pair of jammers. They look like bike shorts without the butt cushion. If you're watching the Olympics right now, all of the male swimmers are wearing them. They're tight, and they go down to just above the knee.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: But when Roy showed up for the test in 2007, he was told no jammers. His bosses at the Office of Parks and Recreation said, you can only do the test in one of the official Jones Beach lifeguard swimsuits, which means you have three choices-- board shorts, trunks, or Speedo. Board shorts and trunks are loose, so nobody really takes a swim test in them because they create more drag and slow you down. So, in effect, state officials were saying to Roy, you have to take the test in the Speedo.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Roy said, no way. I won't do it. And he hasn't been a lifeguard at Jones Beach since.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: It was one of those feelings like, am I making the right decision? I'm throwing away a 40-year career over a principle. It was a difficult decision, a very difficult decision.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: How long did it take you to decide?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: A second.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: I really need to point out he would only have to wear the Speedo for the test, which lasts a minute and 20 seconds. On the job, he'd wear board shorts. Most of the lifeguards do, young and old.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Why not just put it on for the test, though?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Why didn't Rosa Parks just go to the back of the bus? There were plenty of seats.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: So it's just-- it's the principle of it.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Yeah. Yes.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: The principle, in his mind, was standing up to age discrimination. When I read about all this in The New York Times , I really didn't understand. What's the connection between a Speedo and age discrimination? I've certainly seen older dudes in Speedos.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: So I went out and met Roy on a beach not far from his house on Long Island. It was 6:45 in the morning. He was about to go for a mile swim before work.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: So, Roy, can you describe what you're wearing right now?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Well, it's a wet suit. It's a short-sleeve wet suit. And I have my jammers on underneath.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Roy brought one of his official Jones Beach Speedos to the beach to show me.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Just describe it for me.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: It's an exaggerated thong for lack of a better word.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: But it's full coverage in the back. So it's not quite a thong, right?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Not quite a thong, right.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: But to Roy and lots of guys, it might as well be a thong, which is why the Speedo has earned a stable of nicknames-- the weenie bikini, the dingaling sling, the speed don't, the banana hammock, the grape smuggler, the Miami meat tent, the Saint-Tropez truffle duffle, the scrote tote.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: The reason the jammer is preferred by older lifeguards is that you're saying it's more discreet.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Modest.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: More modest?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Than the Speedo.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Because it covers your thighs.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: I don't want to get graphic, but your-- the word begins with B. Basically, you're hanging out with the Speedo.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: I get it now, I think.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: And you don't really-- with the jammers, it's not like that.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: There's like a little bit more of a roof over your house.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Yes. Yes.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: I see.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is the nut of his argument Roy says once he passed 50, he felt self-conscious in the Speedo. And nobody should have to feel self-conscious to get a job. So Roy refuses to put on the grape smuggler to take the swim test.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A few weeks later, there's another chance to take the test. He shows up. And this time, he is wearing the official Speedo. He's just got it on over his jammers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He showed me a video of a conversation he recorded on the pool deck that day. It was a little windy, so the sound isn't great. But he's standing in front of Sue Giuliani who was the director of Jones Beach State Park at the time. And there he is in his jammers plus Speedo outfit, challenging her to turn him away.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: I've made a compromise.

segments.speaker: Sue Giuliani
segments.text: That's not going to be acceptable.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: You're not going to let me swim like this?

segments.speaker: Sue Giuliani
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: How come?

segments.speaker: Sue Giuliani
segments.text: Because you still have jammers on. So that you cannot wear.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: All right. And is there any reason why they're not allowed?

segments.speaker: Sue Giuliani
segments.text: We're not going-- how many times do you want me to repeat it?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Sue Giuliani
segments.text: You know why they're not allowed.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: No, no, I don't. I've never been able to--

segments.speaker: Sue Giuliani
segments.text: I've pretty much--

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Joe Scalise, the director of water safety for the state beaches, cuts in.

segments.speaker: Joe Scalise
segments.text: Are you going to comply or not?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: I am complying. I'm wearing my official suit.

segments.speaker: Joe Scalise
segments.text: Are you complying with what we want or not?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: I'm wearing my official suit.

segments.speaker: Joe Scalise
segments.text: So not swimming now?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: All right. Let's go.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Did you just go home, then?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Basically, I-- well, I stayed around. And I watched everybody take the test.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Were there other people taking the test in jammers?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: No. No, nobody was allowed to take the test in jammers. So everybody else either put on a Speedo or put on the board shorts, something like that.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Now, Roy said he could have worn board shorts or trunks and still pass the test. He says he could have dungarees and passed. The guy's in ridiculous shape. He does triathlons now, coaches a swim team. In 2012, he had a hip replaced. And seven weeks later, he came in first in his age group in Bermuda's Round the Sound swim race, a 1.2-mile open water swim. He was still using a cane to walk.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: So the easy thing for Roy to do would be just take the test in board shorts or Speedo and keep the job he loved. Let bureaucrats be bureaucrats. Just get on with it.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: That's not Roy. Roy does not back down from a fight. So he sued. He sued the New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation for $5 million.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Now, the easy thing for the state would have been to just let Jones Beach lifeguards wear jammers. Presumably, if they're good enough for the Olympic swim team, they're good enough for New York's lifeguards. But that's not New York State. It decided to fight.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: The lawsuit has worked its way through the lower court, which dismissed it, to the appellate court, which ruled in May that it should go to trial. This has been going on for seven years-- seven years. Roy sent me a PDF of his exhibits in the case. It was 1,300 pages long.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: And the thing I really want to know-- because I live in New York and pay taxes in New York-- is why is the state using taxpayer dollars to fight the Speedo suit? This could all been resolved very easily years ago if they just changed the rule, allowed the jammers. Why are Roy and the state fighting each other when they should unite against the real enemy, jellyfish.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Officials from the state of New York wouldn't talk to me for this story. The Attorney General's office wouldn't talk. Neither would Parks and Rec.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: But they did send me the affidavit of a guy named George Gorman. He oversees all the parks in Long Island. And it lays out their side of the story.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Around 2006, some of the Jones Beach lifeguards started taking the test in full-body swimsuits. Management became concerned that those guys were only passing because they were wearing the full-body swimsuits. So they decided to change the rules.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Starting in 2007, lifeguards could only take the test in one of the three official Jones Beach uniform swimsuits. No more full body suits, and also no jammers because jammers aren't part of the uniform. In his deposition, George Gorman said, quote, "we determined it was best that the lifeguards wear the uniforms that they're assigned to wear while they're on duty."

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Seems reasonable, right? Not if you're Roy. He points out, if jammers really are significantly faster, wouldn't you want your lifeguards to wear a faster suit? Get them out to drowning victims sooner?

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: And as it happens, New York Parks and Rec allows lifeguards to take their qualifying test in jammers in the rest of the state.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Upstate. I went upstate to take the test. And I wore my jammers.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: You took the test upstate?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Yes. And I wore my jammers. And people wore the jammers. And I have pictures of that. And it's part of the exhibit, of guys taking the test in their jammers.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Upstate?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Yes. The same employer. New York State Department of Recreation, the same employer, allows the jammers.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: So your theory about this is that they are targeting Long Island because why?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Because 90% of the older, the over-50 lifeguards work on Long Island. It's the biggest group of older lifeguards anywhere.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: For what it's worth, the state told me that the rules are different on Long Island because it's a more strenuous job lifeguarding on the ocean-- upstate it's all lakes and pools.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Why do you think it is that they don't want older lifeguards?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Well, I think they don't like the fact that older lifeguards have influence over the younger guys. And when you're a member of management, you don't want anybody having influence over your employees except you. And when you have to deal with the union, and you have to deal with the offices of the unions who are all older guys, and they know the beach, you don't want that.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Yep, there's a lifeguard union. Roy was the president of the union for years. And at that point in 2007, when he refused to wear the Speedo, he was the union's chief negotiator. When Sue Giuliani tells him to follow the rules--

segments.speaker: Sue Giuliani
segments.text: So that you cannot wear.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: --she knows him. He's the guy the union sends to argue its side. And these guys telling him he can't wear his jammers? They're management. This is a scantily clad labor dispute.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: I asked some other older lifeguards about this. And three out of the four of them agreed. This is about the union, which actually has a history of fighting age discrimination. In 1966, they went on strike because the state tried to impose an age limit of 35 for Jones Beach lifeguards. So they walked off the beach. A week later, the state caved.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Knowing this-- that the suits and the swimsuits have a history with each other-- that helped me understand what Roy's fight was really about. Roy told me one reason he took a stand was that management was supposed to tell the union if they wanted to change a rule like this. And this time, they didn't.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: Roy's got a weekend job now at a private beach club. But it's not the same.

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: I like where I'm working now. I really do. But you get one rescue a year if you're lucky. And then it's what's called a puddle jumper.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: What is a puddle jumper?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: A puddle jumper is where you really don't even need to get your head wet. And at Jones Beach in the old days, we would have these tremendous rescues, just these great rescues.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: His friends from Jones Beach tease him that he's in exile now.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: How often do you go visit them?

segments.speaker: Roy Lester
segments.text: Not that often. I keep in touch with them constantly, but I don't go down there that often. To be honest, it does hurt. It hurts to go down there. That was my beach. It was my home for so many years.

segments.speaker: Dana Chivvis
segments.text: If Roy's theory is true, then the state is trying to get rid of the older lifeguards on Long Island by forcing them into Speedos. But if that's true, as far as I can tell, the only lifeguard they've managed to get rid of is Roy.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dana Chivvis is one of the producers of our show.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [MUSIC - "SPEEDO" BY THE CADILLACS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Two, Say Yes to Summer. So I just finished making a movie with Mike Birbiglia, who is on our show sometimes. And the movie's about improv comedians. And I thought that it would be fun to invite some here on the show to do stuff about summer.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And we got some great ones-- John Lutz, Tami Sagher, Connor Ratliff, Gary Richardson, Kate Micucci, Shannon O'Neill, who's the artistic director of improv theater The Upright Citizens Brigade Theater. Mike Birbiglia came, too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And they did this show at The Upright Citizens Brigade theater in New York. And they did it in this style of improv where the way it works is that somebody tells a true story on stage. And then the performers make up scenes based on things in that real story. And then somebody else tells another true story which kicks off more improvised scenes, and so on.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so, if you just want to picture this, the cast and I are on stage. There's an audience. And we started this show with a true story that I told.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So when I was 13, my parents had enough money to take us on one of our very first family vacations. And we went to Florida. And one of the things that made this possible was we got a deal on the hotel.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: My dad was an accountant. I grew up in Baltimore. And we got the deal because my dad was the accountant for the Baltimore branch franchise of the Playboy Club.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I would just say now it's sort of hard to remember, if you're under 40, I think, there was a point where Playboy was cool. It's sort of unimaginable now. But if you imagine you couldn't get porn on your phone.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so we were going to go down. Playboy owned hotels. And they had a hotel in Miami called the Playboy Plaza. So we were going to be at this hotel that seemed very glamorous. There were going to be Playboy bunnies at the hotel serving drinks at the bar and at the pool. I was a 13-year-old boy. This was incredible.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We were going to fly in an airplane. It was one of the very first times I ever did that-- also incredible. There would be the ocean, which being from Baltimore, we called (IN BALTIMORE ACCENT) the ocean. And so this had all the makings of a great vacation.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then when we got to the hotel, it was everything we wanted. And in addition, The Jackson 5 was staying there. August of 1972, Michael Jackson and I are the same age. We were both 13.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so you would see The Jackson 5 come out of the elevator for dinner, dressed all in completely matching gold suede suits with fringe. And you would see them at the pool just like playing in the pool like other kids, which was us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I should say, I remember goofing around in the pool with the youngest one, who was seven years old-- a girl-- because she seemed like the most approachable. I knew she wasn't actually famous. Later, of course, I learned she is Janet Jackson. I played Marco Polo with Janet Jackson.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I have brought with me a photo of me and Michael Jackson from that vacation. I have it here. Now before I show this to you, I want to just-- I need to preface with some context, which is that while the Jacksons were becoming international superstars, I myself was working in the entertainment business. I had gone to the Baltimore County Public Library and taken out some books on how to do magic tricks. And I was doing birthday parties all over Baltimore County for fees as high as $10-- also animal balloonery.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so here is the photo. And the audience here can see that my back is to the camera. What I'm doing-- you can't see my hands. I'm doing the disappearing coin trick. And the expression on Michael Jackson's face? He is literally rolling his eyes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So just to explain to the radio audience, the cast is sitting on stools with microphones. And so you guys heard the opening story. It's on you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, a dad tries something he has never done before, one summer with his family. That's in a minute on Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life . I'm Ira Glass. Each week on our program, of course, we choose a theme, bring you different stories on that theme. Today's show, My Summer Self, stories of who we are during the summer. We've arrived at Act Three of our show. Act Three, It Takes a Villa.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So sometimes during the summer, people just decide they are going to try and do things they never do, go on some adventure, attempt something, and just see if it takes, see if this is who they are, see if they are the kind of summery person they have never been till now. One of our producers, Neil Drumming, witnessed his dad make an attempt like that.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: In the summer of 1982, my dad did something unexpected, something that seemed unbelievably indulgent. He took me, my mom, and my brother, and the youngest of my three sisters on the most epic road trip any of us could have possibly imagined at the time. We piled into my dad's Buick Skylark and drove from Queens, New York to the World's Fair in Knoxville, Tennessee, where a robot danced for us, and then down into Orlando, Florida.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: This was a big deal. Before this, going away meant visiting relatives in South Carolina and sitting uncomfortably among aunts and second cousins whose names I would forget before we'd even pulled out of their dusty driveways. This trip was not country heat and sipping sugar water on some rickety porch while listening to the inscrutable conversation of grown folk. It was what going 1,000 miles from home should feel like.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: We cruised down a brightly lit street called International Drive. We stayed at a Holiday Inn taller and more grand than any I'd ever seen. Sunlight streamed in through a hole in the ceiling, a hole that was supposed to be there.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Our parents took us to a building that looked like a pile of poached eggs, but was actually Xanadu, House of the Future. And everywhere, along every roadside, billboards promised that the most magical scene still awaited us, this place, Disney World. By all accounts, it was paradise for kids.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: But between the gas and the hotels and the eating out, my dad quickly discovered how expensive taking even 60% of his brood on a Disney vacation could be. He was resigned to do it, but he wasn't above working the angles. He found out that you could get cheap tickets to the Magic Kingdom if you just signed up to sit through an hour or so spiel from someone pitching timeshares. He was in.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: The hard sell went down at the Disney Village, a branded mini mall near the famous theme park. My mom, dad, and a handful of other determined parents stowed their kids in a room full of toys that had been conveniently provided by the salespeople. The parents set about the business of listening-- or not-- waiting patiently for the moment when the closers would stop shilling and start handing out the Disney discounts.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: But while we kids were in another room throwing LEGOs at one another, something surprising happened. My dad bit. He went into a closed room to get three-day passes just so that I could eventually lose my glasses on Space Mountain. And he came out with a deed, the deed to something he and my mom were now calling our villa.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: My father was a bold man, but in retrospect this is the most impetuous action that I have ever seen him take. It cost him about $5,000, which he paid in installments. In 1982, for a guy with five kids who never made more than $33,000 a year at his day job, it was a considerable investment.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: For those unfamiliar with timeshares, it may be hard to wrap your head around buying a vacation home that you never really own. You pay upfront for it. There's an annual maintenance fee. But you only get to stay in it once a year or so, usually for a week at a time. It almost sounds like some sort of scam. And sometimes it is. But it didn't turn out that way for us. Instead, it became a fixture in my family.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: My father had chosen as our week the first week in July. And so every year, during one of the hottest months of the year, we would head down I-95 as always. But now, when we pulled into South Carolina to see relatives, that was only a pit stop on the way to our true destination. We had transformed from people who went away to a family who went on vacation.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Our villa was number 317, a two-bedroom apartment with an enclosed back porch that looked out onto a small man-made lake complete with fish and ducks and another summer word that I learned, gazebo. My brother chased cicadas and lizards. For my sister, the only swimmer among my siblings, there was a pool. There were tennis courts and bikes to rent. The general store even offered a collection of the latest movies on laser disc.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: That first trip, I was eight. As I got older, I moved from the gazebo to the game room and then the gym, trying to meet other kids my age. My mom busied herself in the kitchen making lunches or sat by the lake and watched the ducks. My dad shepherded us through It's a Small World and Epcot Center.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Our summers went on like this, pretty much exactly like this, probably until I finished high school. I honestly loved it. I looked forward to this trip every year. And even though it was only a week, it was almost always the highlight of my entire summer.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: But when I think about it now, it occurs to me my dad pretty much orchestrated this thing that became so important to our lives. And I have no idea whether or not he ever enjoyed it himself. In fact, it didn't seem like he did. I can't recall actually seeing him happy.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Neither does my brother. He says dad was pretty much the same at the timeshare as he was at home. Sometimes he'd go for walks alone, but often he just sat on the couch and watched TV. I asked my sister. She said he must have been happy, but she doesn't remember witnessing it, either.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: It seems like such a simple question, but I just wanted to know. Did he enjoy himself?

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: At the risk of embodying the most tired trope in all of modern masculinity, I will say my father and I never really got along. He was strict. His house had a lot of rules. And he believed in corporal punishment. And the sting of that conflict stayed with me as an adult. But since my mom passed away last year, I've been trying to connect with him more. I gave him a call.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: [TELEPHONE RINGING]

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yes?

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Hey, it's Neil.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Is it a bad time?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: It's about who?

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: I say, is it a bad time?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: No. No, I was just playing solitaire. Yeah. I didn't know whether it was the drugstore or not.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Are you waiting for a call from the drugstore?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: No. They'll call. They'll give me a call no matter when it is.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: My dad is 83 years old now and living alone in Florida. Talking to him can be awkward and not just because his hearing is going. I asked him point blank if he liked going to the villa. He told me that when he was growing up, he barely ever left South Carolina.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: I didn't know nothing about nothing else. You know, like, you saw things in magazines and stuff. The first time I knew about a dentist I was in the army. But I just thought it was a good idea that our kids see something other than their surroundings and where they were born.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: My dad grew up poor on a farm, one of 12 children. He says he only finished high school because by the time he was old enough, he was the one driving the bus. Sometimes when there were athletic events at other schools, he'd get to drive the teams and learn what the nearby towns were like.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In 1953, he was drafted into the army, which had only recently been integrated. They sent him to Colorado and Indiana. And it wasn't great. He says the army was really not into black people back then.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So those were his travel experiences when he was young. I was hearing a lot of this for the first time. As it turns out, that's at least partially my own fault.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: The reason why we never talk about it because it just wasn't the kind of thing that you guys seemed to be interested in.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Really? So we just didn't seem like we were interested as kids?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yeah. Right.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Yeah, I probably wasn't so interested back then, back when the two of us were constantly challenging each other. I was always either afraid of him or angry at him, hiding from him or planting my feet to confront him. It never crossed my mind to try to understand him.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: But nowadays my dad feels to me like some kind of living cold case, a million-page brief that is no longer redacted. Maybe it's because I'm now at the age he was when I was born, but I retroactively find his every decision fascinating, even the ones that aren't so surprising on the surface.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Why Florida?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: It was advertised. And you get to hear something about Florida. And then this thing, Disney World. After we started going, they build Epcot. They build Animal Kingdom. And they advertise them a lot.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Not many people were going. We were probably the most vacationing people in our area. I don't know of any other family that went on vacation every year. We did.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: My dad was obviously proud that he got the timeshare. But pride, strictly speaking, does not constitute joy. It didn't answer the question of whether or not he was actually happy spending those summer weeks with us at the villa. Instead, he kept trying to make me understand why he brought us there in the first place. And his explanation, his reasoning, reached back to memories and past experiences that not only had I never heard, but that kind of blew my mind.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Now, I tell you, probably where I got the whole idea, when we went to school, every summer you had to try to think of something that you could write about when you go back to school because you're going to have to write something about what you did this summer. Well, we never had anything to write about when I was going to school. And you didn't think plowing a mule, or picking peaches or stuff, that you had to normally do, you didn't think that was so exciting to write about. And so we made up lies about what we did.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Well, every summer you guys went on vacation, you could write about something that you did or saw or some place you went.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Yeah. What did you do during the summers?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: When? This year?

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: No, no, when you were in school.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Worked. That's what I tried to tell you.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: We talked for over an hour. It was one of the longest conversations that I can remember us ever having. Every now and then, I try to steer him back to the question I wanted him to answer.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: So I know I asked you this a bunch of times. I keep asking you the same question. You can tell me to stop asking you if you want, but did you have fun yourself?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yeah. See, I don't regret anything because it looked to me like I was doing what I was supposed to do. And to see your kids happy was to be happy, too. And you guys could always come in and do whatever it is and go back out to the pool or whatever. I remember you guys playing out there and hanging around the bushes and stuff. I thought it was great.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: That's the kind of enjoyment I hadn't considered. I live more selfishly. Also, his answer was hard to take in, to reconcile with the distance I felt between us at the time, back when he would retire to the couch to watch TV while we went off to play on our own. Maybe he was watching me play in the bushes and getting a kick out of it. But I didn't know that.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Still, I was happy at the villa. And my dad says he was, too. I'm glad I know that.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: All right. So I've been talking to you for an hour. I should probably let you go. But, hey, is it OK if I call back this week and just talk? I want to hear more stuff. Since I didn't seem interested when I was a kid, I didn't realize that was why you didn't tell us stuff. So now I'll just ask. Is that OK if I could--

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: The only thing I'd do is to get up and sometimes I'm outside just walking around. Sometimes I sit down and-- sometimes I go ride the bike. And I do this just to keep busy. You can call me anytime--

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: All right. I'm going to go back to work.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Bye, Dad.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Bye.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Neil Drumming, one of the producers of our show.
